title: Larry's New Love

jokes.text: Larry interrupts Paul Westerberg's performance to ask who he's waving at, then responds to 'the girl in the front row' with 'Wow. Nice rack.'
jokes.setup: Paul Westerberg waves mid-song during a live on-air performance; Larry, curious, asks who he's waving at
jokes.punchline: Larry's response to learning it's the girl in the front row is the unfiltered, utterly inappropriate 'Wow. Nice rack.' — pure Larry id leaking through the professional veneer
jokes.explanation: Perfectly distills Larry's character: the professional host who can't suppress his lizard-brain impulses even on live television. The interruption of a sincere musical performance for this shallow observation is a master class in Larry's self-absorption. High character integration because no other character on TV would deliver this so nakedly during a live broadcast.

jokes.text: After Larry says 'Nice rack,' Westerberg reveals 'That's Alex' — the girl is Larry's girlfriend — and Larry, unfazed, repeats 'Nice rack.'
jokes.setup: Larry says 'Nice rack' about a random girl. Westerberg reveals she's someone Larry knows — his girlfriend Alex.
jokes.punchline: Larry simply repeats 'Nice rack' — the revelation changes nothing for him, which is the whole joke
jokes.explanation: The callback lands harder than the original joke. The structure is near-perfect: setup expectation that the revelation will embarrass Larry, then the punchline is that he's completely unashamed and just repeats himself. It's absurdist in its economy — two words do all the work. Deeply character-specific: Larry's narcissism means his girlfriend's physical attributes exist for his approval regardless of context. The repeat is funnier than any new line could be.

jokes.text: Artie tells Larry the last 6 weeks have been his best shows in years because he's happy. Larry says he's been 'feeling something lately' and couldn't identify it. Artie tells him the word: 'Happy!'
jokes.setup: Artie attributes Larry's professional peak to happiness. Larry genuinely cannot recognize his own emotional state.
jokes.punchline: Larry has been experiencing happiness for weeks and lacked the self-awareness to name it — Artie has to tell him
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed character joke about Larry's pathological emotional disconnection. The comedy is in the specificity — Larry doesn't just lack self-awareness, he literally cannot identify his own positive emotions without a producer labeling them. Earns its impact through character truth rather than a twist.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I've been Feeling something Lately. I couldn't put my finger On it. Maybe it's that-- What'd you call it? Happy!

jokes.text: Artie says 'Happy! 10 kisses, shortest one, one long as 20' — apparently a nonsensical rhyme or toast — to which Larry replies 'Yeah, why don't you go get a costume and come back?'
jokes.setup: Artie is exuberantly celebrating Larry's happiness with an odd, theatrical proclamation
jokes.punchline: Larry's deadpan dismissal — 'go get a costume and come back' — treats Artie's enthusiasm as an unwanted performance
jokes.explanation: Artie's proclamation is deliberately baffling, and Larry's response is a solid deflation. The joke works mainly on Rip Torn's energy versus Shandling's tired tolerance. Not exceptional but functional — captures the dynamic between the two men.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Hey, do you think When I come out To do the monologue, I should just rush To the front of the stage And shake everyone's hand The way Leno does?

jokes.text: Larry floats the idea of rushing to the front of the stage and shaking everyone's hand 'the way Leno does.' Artie ignores this completely, handing him keys and a credit card.
jokes.setup: Larry asks if he should mimic Leno's crowd-greeting technique
jokes.punchline: Artie treats the question as nonexistent — doesn't dignify it with a response, just redirects to logistics — implying it's too stupid to engage with
jokes.explanation: Classic Larry Sanders Show technique: the non-answer as answer. Larry's insecurity about Leno is a series throughline, and Artie's complete dismissal is funnier than any verbal rejection. The industry-insider specificity (Leno's crowd greeting) adds texture.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yeah, he's still Got to take Hank apart And put him back In the box.

jokes.text: Artie declines coming to dinner: 'A producer's day is never done.' Larry immediately: 'Yeah, he's still got to take Hank apart and put him back in the box.'
jokes.setup: Artie gives an earnest reason for not joining dinner
jokes.punchline: Larry reframes Artie's evening as the mechanical act of disassembling and storing Hank like a toy — reducing Hank to a managed object rather than a person
jokes.explanation: Wonderfully dark and specific to the show's world. The image of Hank being 'put back in the box' like an action figure perfectly encapsulates the show's view of Hank as a managed personality rather than a real person. Economy is excellent — maximum cruelty in minimum words. The joke also works because Alex is present as a newcomer hearing the casual contempt for a colleague.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Why, are you quitting?

jokes.text: Alex says everyone likes her. Larry immediately says 'Really? I like everyone.' — suggesting he's the anomaly, not her
jokes.setup: Alex notes that Larry's colleagues like her
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'I like everyone' implies this is somehow remarkable or out of character — a self-aware admission that he's normally difficult
jokes.explanation: Mild but real. The self-aware admission plays nicely as a honeymoon-phase version of Larry — he's being charming about his own difficult nature. Not strong enough to be memorable but lands cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Alex
dialogue.line: I don't usually hear that Until my pants are off.

jokes.text: After Hank says 'You're a lucky man, Mr. Larry Sanders,' Larry responds: 'Why, are you quitting?'
jokes.setup: Hank delivers what's meant as a compliment about Larry's luck in having Alex
jokes.punchline: Larry instantly reframes 'lucky man' as good news about losing Hank — suggesting Hank leaving would be the real stroke of luck
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. Three words do devastating work: Larry doesn't need to insult Hank — he just recontextualizes 'lucky' to mean 'free of Hank.' The structure is textbook misdirection executed with maximum economy. Deeply character-specific: only Larry would respond to a compliment this way, and only in relation to Hank. Quotable and rewatchable. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor example.

jokes.punchline: Beverly's response — 'I don't usually hear that until my pants are off' — reframes the interaction as sexual without explanation
jokes.explanation: A functional raunchy non-sequitur. Beverly's delivery would carry this, but the joke itself isn't particularly original — it's a 'this sounds sexual out of context' setup that's well-worn territory. Works as a character beat (Beverly is sardonic) but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Alex suggests the mermaid sketch is 'a little Benny Hill' for having a man dress as a woman. Larry, clearly never having considered this, slowly turns to the camera/room: 'That's what we are. We are Benny Hill.'
jokes.setup: Alex diplomatically critiques the drag element of the sketch as dated
jokes.punchline: Larry's dawning horror as he processes that his prestigious late-night show might share DNA with lowbrow British comedy — and his genuine, appalled acceptance of this
jokes.explanation: Works on multiple levels: it's industry self-critique (late-night comedy's reliance on drag is low-hanging fruit), it's Larry's vanity being punctured by someone he's trying to impress, and it's a callback to the kind of insecurity the show always mines. 'That's what we are. We ARE Benny Hill' lands because of the repetition and Larry's apparent genuine crisis.

jokes.text: After pitching improvements to the sketch, Alex says 'You know, I could play that part' — then immediately stops herself, mortified. 'I'm sorry. Oh, god. Of the, uh... I'm sorry. That was so just... Presumptuous.'
jokes.setup: Alex has been diplomatically workshopping the sketch with Larry. She gets carried away.
jokes.punchline: She catches herself mid-sentence having essentially auditioned for a role on her new boyfriend's show — the social horror of the moment lands in her self-flagellating spiral
jokes.explanation: A well-observed cringe moment — the specific social horror of accidentally revealing ambition to someone who can fulfill it. The comedy is in the spiraling self-correction. Gains a rewatch bonus because it seeds the entire episode's conflict about Alex's career motivations.

jokes.text: Larry tells Alex she should do the mermaid sketch: 'Because I'm never going to be able to talk Hank into going up into that bed and breakfast with me and I think I have a shot with you.'
jokes.setup: Alex is embarrassed about pitching herself for the sketch; Larry says he thinks she should do it
jokes.punchline: His reason — that he's given up on getting Hank to go to a bed and breakfast with him — is a completely insane non-sequitur that reveals more questions than it answers
jokes.explanation: Brilliant in its absurdity: Larry's logic for casting Alex is that he's tried and failed to seduce Hank into a romantic getaway. The joke works because it (a) implies an entire failed history of Larry-Hank B&B scheming, (b) reframes his relationship with Alex as essentially 'you're the Hank who'll go,' and (c) is delivered with complete earnestness. High character integration — this is uniquely Larry's warped reasoning.

jokes.punchline: Larry's response suggests he and his ass are separate entities deserving separate salutations — the joke implies the ass might be the greater one
jokes.explanation: Quick, functional joke on Larry's vanity vs. self-deprecation. The punchline works better if the ass is genuinely something Artie might prioritize greeting — which, in the show's world, is not entirely implausible. Solid economy, slightly predictable structure.

jokes.text: Larry asks if 'that drunk guy from Chicago' (Ed Wallace) is coming. Artie: 'No. He doesn't drink anymore.' Larry: 'Oh, thank god. That guy really needed to get that under control.' Artie: 'No, I mean he stopped drinking because he fell into Lake Michigan and drowned.'
jokes.setup: Larry's relief that the drunk affiliate guy has sobered up sets up an expectation of a reformed character
jokes.punchline: He didn't sober up — he died. The 'not drinking anymore' was because death ended the habit
jokes.explanation: A beautifully dark misdirection. The structure is clean: sobriety is set up as the punchline, then death is the real punchline. The extended setup (Larry's earnest approval of Ed's recovery) makes the reveal hit harder. Very much in the Larry Sanders Show register — casual cruelty delivered without drama. The follow-up '12 steps' joke elevates it further.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Oh, god. Which of the 12 steps is that?' Artie: 'The last one.'
jokes.setup: They've just established that Ed Wallace drowned. Larry asks which AA step 'falling into a lake and drowning' corresponds to.
jokes.punchline: 'The last one' — death as the terminal step of recovery
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum payload. 'The last one' is one of the most economical dark jokes possible — it reframes the AA framework as having a final, terminal step that nobody discusses. The structure built by Joke 15 allows this to land with almost no additional setup. Highly quotable out of context. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in economy and darkness; exceeds it slightly in structural perfection.

jokes.text: After establishing that Ed Wallace drowned, Artie notes it's a shame because 'we're doing the mermaid sketch and Ed always chuckled at that one.'
jokes.setup: A man has just drowned. Artie's concern pivots to the sketch about underwater creatures.
jokes.punchline: Artie mourns the drowning victim primarily as a lost audience member for the mermaid sketch — the dark irony of a drowned man's fondness for mermaid content
jokes.explanation: The mermaid sketch connecting to a drowning death is a mordant coincidence that the show plays completely straight. Artie's total lack of sentimentality about the death — only caring about the lost chuckle — is peak Larry Sanders Show worldbuilding. The joke requires no winking; it's the writers' confidence that makes it land.

jokes.text: Larry tells Artie he asked Alex to play the mermaid. Artie's barely disguised reaction: 'Hipper, huh? Ha ha. Uh! I see.'
jokes.setup: Larry casually mentions he's replaced Hank in the mermaid sketch with his new girlfriend
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'Hipper, huh? Ha ha. Uh! I see.' is an entire performance of barely suppressed professional concern masquerading as casual acceptance — the 'Uh!' is doing enormous work
jokes.explanation: Rip Torn's reaction beat is where this lives — the transcript captures enough of it (the 'Uh!' the 'I see') to score it. Artie immediately sees the political disaster Larry has just created but can't say so outright. The comedy is in the gap between what Artie says and what he means.

jokes.text: Artie asks 'Well, can she act?' about Alex. Larry: 'It's the mermaid sketch.'
jokes.setup: Artie raises a legitimate professional concern about whether Larry's girlfriend can perform
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'It's the mermaid sketch' dismisses the concern entirely — implying the sketch is so low-bar that acting ability is irrelevant
jokes.explanation: Economy does heavy lifting here — Larry's four-word dismissal both defends Alex and inadvertently insults the sketch's artistic merit. The implicit self-deprecation about the quality of their own content is classic Larry Sanders Show.

jokes.text: Hank says he's been told he won't be playing the mermaid. He protests: 'People know me as the mermaid.' The writer responds: 'I know, but I'm sorry. That's the way it is.'
jokes.setup: Hank receives the news that his defining sketch role has been stripped
jokes.punchline: Hank's identity claim — 'people know me as the mermaid' — is both pathetically self-aggrandizing (as if this is his legacy) and genuinely sad. The writer's flat acceptance makes it worse.
jokes.explanation: The tragedy-comedy of Hank Kingsley in microcosm: his most cherished identity marker is being a recurring mermaid character. Tambor would play this with devastating earnestness. The joke is in the gap between Hank's perceived importance and how he's actually perceived.

dialogue.speaker: Larry

jokes.text: Hank warns there's 'something behind her eyes' about Alex. The writer responds: 'That would be her brain, Hank, an organ that you may not be familiar with.'
jokes.setup: Hank delivers a vague, ominous warning about Alex: 'there's something behind her eyes'
jokes.punchline: The writer clarifies it's a brain — implying Hank wouldn't recognize one from proximity
jokes.explanation: Crisp structure: Hank's portentous non-observation is deflated by the literal answer followed by the insult. The dig at Hank's intelligence is character-earned — Hank's intellectual limitations are a running subtext. 'An organ that you may not be familiar with' is a clean, well-constructed insult.

jokes.setup: Hank has been thoroughly insulted and his protest about Alex dismissed
jokes.punchline: His only response is a solitary 'Fuck.' — the defeated profanity of a man who has no counter-argument
jokes.explanation: One word, perfectly placed. Tambor's single 'Fuck' after the brain insult is a complete emotional statement — acceptance, defeat, and wounded pride in one syllable. The humor is in the total deflation after Hank's ominous buildup. The 10-second gap in the transcript ([07:07] to [07:17]) suggests a long beat after the word.

jokes.text: Hank introduces the mermaid sketch on-air: 'Tonight the mermaid will be played by a lovely and talented lady instead of me.' The audience laughs at the 'instead of me.'
jokes.setup: Hank must professionally introduce the segment from which he's been replaced
jokes.punchline: He editorializes with 'instead of me' — making his displacement visible to the audience and turning his humiliation into a passive-aggressive public statement
jokes.explanation: Peak Hank Kingsley behavior: the inability to suppress his wounded ego even in a professional context. 'Instead of me' is an elegant piece of passive aggression that simultaneously generates audience sympathy and exposes his pettiness. The studio audience laughing (noted in transcript) validates this as a landing moment. Deep character integration — only Hank would do this.

jokes.setup: The sketch parodies domestic sitcom phone-call conventions in an underwater setting
jokes.punchline: The underwater domestic equivalent of 'doorbell' is 'anchor and chain' — the logical extension of the mermaid world's domestic life
jokes.explanation: A competent sketch joke — the underwater domestic life parody is functional but the specific joke is mild. The anchor-and-chain detail is logical but not particularly surprising. Gets the job done within the sketch's frame.

jokes.explanation: A functional sketch-comedy pun. 'Blow-hole' works as anatomical/marine wordplay and as a euphemism simultaneously. Not exceptional but lands cleanly. The mermaid sketch overall reads as deliberate mediocrity — the show is satirizing this kind of sketch, which makes individual jokes within it less impressive.

jokes.explanation: A solid piece of absurdist wordplay in the sketch — the mermaid world's version of a mundane domestic expression. Clever enough but not exceptional; it's sketch-within-a-show humor which has lower stakes.

jokes.text: Hank appears on stage during Alex's mermaid sketch to protest: 'You're probably wondering why I'm not playing the mermaid, right?' then insists 'I am the mermaid.' The audience laughs.
jokes.setup: Alex is performing the mermaid sketch. Hank apparently intrudes on-camera mid-sketch to voice his objection
jokes.punchline: Hank breaking the fiction of the sketch to assert his mermaid identity to the live audience — prioritizing his wounded pride over the live broadcast
jokes.explanation: Hank sabotaging a live segment to reclaim his mermaid identity is the escalation of everything set up earlier. The show lets Hank be genuinely unhinged here — 'I AM the mermaid' is both the funniest and most tragic thing he could say. This is the episode's comedic peak for the Hank storyline and Tambor's finest moment in the episode. 'I am the mermaid' is genuinely quotable.

jokes.text: Hank, having crashed the sketch: 'Look at that. I mean, look at her. I mean, do you really buy that she has ever been underwater? Huh? I don't. I'm sorry, I don't.'
jokes.setup: Hank is on-stage during Alex's mermaid sketch, having already announced his protest to the audience
jokes.punchline: His critique of Alex's aquatic credibility — 'do you really buy that she has ever been underwater?' — as if being convincingly 'underwater' is the central performance challenge
jokes.explanation: Hank applying legitimate-sounding casting critique ('has she ever been underwater?') to a mermaid sketch is peak absurdist Hank logic. His wounded repetition ('I'm sorry, I don't') adds the cringe layer. The joke works because Hank genuinely believes this is a valid professional objection.

jokes.text: The mermaid sketch joke: 'They can eat anything. They're so lucky, and you don't hear people standing around saying, "Look how fat that whale got."'
jokes.setup: Within the mermaid sketch, they're talking about whales eating people
jokes.punchline: The observation that whales are immune to body-shaming — nobody fat-shames a whale — spun as envy
jokes.explanation: A reasonably inventive observational joke within the sketch, but the character integration is low (it could be in any sketch), and the structure is loose. The sketch-within-a-show framing means individual sketch jokes carry less weight — they're meant to be somewhat mediocre by design.

jokes.text: Alex asks for a video cassette of the show by 'tomorrow' so she can give it to her agent. Beverly, mid-cheerful-agreement, freezes when she processes this.
jokes.setup: Alex has been charming and grateful; Beverly has been accommodating. Alex reveals the tape is for her agent.
jokes.punchline: Beverly's audible deep sigh ('Mmm!') after Alex leaves — registering that Alex's warmth was at least partly instrumental. Beverly instantly understands what Larry may not yet.
jokes.explanation: Beverly's sigh is a classic Larry Sanders Show reaction beat — a non-verbal line reading that carries the show's cynical worldview. It doesn't need dialogue. Beverly is the audience surrogate who sees through the LA bullshit instantly. Gains rewatch value because it foreshadows the episode's central conflict.

jokes.text: Larry spots Warren Littlefield (NBC president) at a party and says 'I'm hoping he doesn't see me.' Artie: 'It's too late.'
jokes.setup: Larry wants to avoid the NBC president — professional awkwardness at a social event
jokes.punchline: Artie's flat 'It's too late' — confirming Larry's social anxiety is about to be tested with no escape
jokes.explanation: A reliable comedic structure — character states wish, immediately denied. Works on economy and the industry-specific context of late-night competition anxiety. Not particularly inventive but functions well.

jokes.text: Littlefield tells Larry that Jay Leno 'sends his best.' Larry responds by saying he loves Leno's new audience-greeting bit — 'That was my idea.' Littlefield: 'It's still good.'
jokes.setup: Warren mentions Leno, which triggers Larry's competitive insecurity
jokes.punchline: Larry claims credit for Leno's signature move; Warren's polite 'It's still good' dismisses the claim without directly contradicting it — the most cutting possible response
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure: Larry claiming authorship of a competitor's signature move, then Littlefield's 'It's still good' — the 'still' implying 'despite you not doing it' or 'despite the claim being insane' — is a perfect passive-aggressive put-down. The callback to Larry's earlier Leno obsession gives it added resonance. 'It's still good' is the kind of line that could only land in this world.

jokes.text: Roger Bingham interrupts by announcing 'counter-programming' — 'We've got a thing called must pee tv.'
jokes.setup: Roger crashes the Larry-Warren exchange with industry bravado
jokes.punchline: 'Must pee TV' — a parody of NBC's 'Must See TV' branding, reframing appointment television as a biological necessity
jokes.explanation: A solid industry-insider pun — 'must pee TV' is amusing and requires context knowledge that HBO viewers of this era would have. Not exceptional but earns its moment.

jokes.text: Roger tells Alex 'you were really funny tonight' and she jokes 'I guess that means I get my own show.' Roger laughs. Larry: 'She can have mine for 10 bucks.'
jokes.setup: Alex makes a self-deprecating joke about her mermaid performance leading to a show
jokes.punchline: Larry offers his show for $10 — a moment of genuine self-deprecation or paranoid deflection dressed as a joke
jokes.explanation: The '$10' specificity is what makes this work — not 'she can have mine' but the ridiculous low price, implying the show is worth less than nothing to Larry in this moment. Also seeds the episode's anxieties about show ownership and replacement. Dark self-deprecation that only Larry would perform publicly.

jokes.text: Alex reveals that Roger Bingham invited her to the San Francisco network affiliate event. Larry processes this. 'Well, that'll be fun.' Alex: 'Larry, it's business, you know. It's a big chance for me, don't you think?'
jokes.setup: Alex mentions she's going to San Francisco for the affiliate event — the same event where Roger has been discussing replacing Larry
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'Well, that'll be fun' — an attempt at supportive normalcy while clearly computing the betrayal — is the joke, followed by his visible shutdown
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Larry's barely maintained surface calm while clearly spiraling underneath. 'Well, that'll be fun' is a performance of supportiveness so thin it functions as comedy. The cringe comes from watching both characters navigate this without saying what's actually happening.

jokes.text: In the affiliate meeting, Larry dismisses concerns about midwest ratings: 'That's because they have a lot of twisters there. You got shit flying around. You're not gonna be watching tv.'
jokes.setup: Network execs note that Larry's numbers are soft in the midwest
jokes.punchline: Larry attributes midwest viewership dips to tornado activity — as if weather-related distraction is the real demographic problem
jokes.explanation: A sharply funny deflection that reveals Larry's Manhattan/LA insulation — his theory that tornado season explains midwest numbers is absurd but delivered with total confidence. 'You got shit flying around' is the kind of line Shandling would nail. Works as character comedy and as mild geographic satire.

jokes.text: Roger says he wants to see 'a little more of Alex in the show' because she brings 'a female energy' — and then trails off: '...She's very sexy.' Larry: 'Is that your thought or—'
jokes.setup: Roger offers professional-sounding reasons to feature Alex more: feminine energy, freshness, excitement
jokes.punchline: He can't maintain the professional framing and lands on 'She's very sexy' — immediately puncturing the business rationale with naked attraction. Larry's 'Is that your thought or—' implies he sees through it.
jokes.explanation: The joke tracks a familiar Hollywood pattern — the executive who constructs business language around personal desire. Roger's 'we all kind of came up with it at the same time' when pressed is a perfect corporate weasel response. Larry's 'Is that your thought or—' with Artie cutting him off is a masterclass in interrupted comedy — the funniest punchline is the one we don't get to hear.

jokes.text: When pressed on whether 'she's very sexy' is his thought, Roger says 'We all kind of came up with it at the same time.' Then immediately: 'If you want me to take credit for it, I'd be happy to.'
jokes.setup: Roger has been caught reducing his network note to 'she's sexy'
jokes.punchline: His weaseling — 'we all came up with it' — followed by instantly offering to take sole credit if that's helpful — reveals a man with absolutely no stable position
jokes.explanation: The pivot from collective responsibility to eager individual credit is a precise skewering of network executive logic. Roger is simultaneously covering himself and offering to expose himself — which is politically incoherent and therefore funny. Good character-specific comedy about LA power dynamics.

jokes.text: Artie forcibly ends the meeting: 'All right! Wonderful meeting! Yes!' cutting off Larry's interrogation of Roger.
jokes.setup: Larry is about to confront Roger about whose thought 'she's sexy' was; the room is about to blow up
jokes.punchline: Artie's theatrical 'All right! Wonderful meeting! Yes!' — producer damage control as performance art — abruptly terminates the confrontation
jokes.explanation: The 'wonderful meeting' trope is well-worn, but Artie's specific use of it here — saving Larry from himself — is character-specific. Rip Torn's theatrical enthusiasm as a shield is one of the show's recurring pleasures.

jokes.text: After the meeting, Roger tells Artie to 'have that suit tested' — apparently Artie's suit is ridiculous enough to warrant market research. 'Ha ha ha!'
jokes.setup: The meeting is wrapping up with industry pleasantries
jokes.punchline: Roger's parting shot about Artie's suit being subject to testing — implying it's so outlandish it registers as a problem — is a visual gag we can't see but can infer
jokes.explanation: A visual gag entirely dependent on what Artie is wearing, which we can't assess. Functions as a mild character beat — Artie's old-school showbiz aesthetic is an ongoing texture — but without the visual, it's a minor moment.

jokes.text: Larry tells Artie to call the network and threaten to take the show elsewhere unless Roger is removed. Artie: 'That's a call I should make, man. No, no, no. You'll end up saying something you'll regret. I'll do it.'
jokes.setup: Larry wants to personally call the network to get Roger fired
jokes.punchline: Artie's intervention — and particularly 'you'll end up saying something you'll regret' — is both protective and an acknowledgment that Larry cannot be trusted with his own professional crises
jokes.explanation: A competent character beat — Artie as the adult Larry never had. The implication that Larry is known to say regrettable things in professional calls is well-established character shorthand. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Slap on your shelled bra, little mermaid. You're back in business.'
jokes.setup: Artie is telling Hank that the situation has reversed — Hank will be back in the mermaid sketch
jokes.punchline: Artie's choice of words — 'shelled bra, little mermaid' — is a theatrical, affectionate diminutive that also reasserts Hank's most pathetic identity
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback that closes the Hank/mermaid thread with wit. 'Little mermaid' is endearingly condescending, and 'shelled bra' is a specific, funny image. Artie's delivery would be warm but barely concealing amusement. One of the episode's most quotable lines.

jokes.text: Artie tells Larry to remember his 'true love': 'Every night, the show is here for you. Everything else is bullshit.'
jokes.setup: Artie is consoling Larry about the Roger situation and the Alex complications
jokes.punchline: Artie's version of emotional support is to remind Larry that his only real relationship is with a television show — 'everything else is bullshit' — which is both darkly funny and probably true
jokes.explanation: This is the show's thesis statement delivered as a joke. 'The show is here for you. Everything else is bullshit.' is darkly romantic and perfectly captures Larry's pathology — and Artie's complete, unsentimental understanding of it. The comedy is in Artie presenting this as obvious wisdom rather than an indictment. High character integration — Artie as the enabler of Larry's show-as-relationship worldview.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I can't lose this show, Artie.' Artie responds: 'I'm gonna put Jon Stewart in there, if it's the last thing I do.'
jokes.setup: Artie is supposed to be supporting Larry against Roger's attempt to replace him with Jon Stewart
jokes.punchline: Artie's line sounds like a threat — 'I'm gonna put Jon Stewart in there' — before context clarifies he means it as a counter-threat toward Roger, but the misreading of the line is briefly funny
jokes.explanation: The Jon Stewart namedrop is an interesting industry-specific moment (Stewart was genuinely ascending at this time), but the joke itself is ambiguous and not particularly sharp. The misdirection of Artie sounding like he's siding with Roger is mild.

jokes.text: After the Alex breakup-adjacent conversation, Larry tells her: 'You know, San Francisco's really, uh, very nice.' Alex: 'Is it?' Larry: 'Yeah. Maybe you'll take me sometime.'
jokes.setup: Alex has decided not to go to San Francisco, apparently to keep peace with Larry. The tension has slightly resolved.
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately reopens the wound by suggesting she take him to San Francisco — essentially inviting himself on the very trip she just sacrificed, revealing his emotional processing is entirely self-referential
jokes.explanation: A quietly devastating character moment that functions as dark comedy. Larry is so solipsistic that his 'making up' involves proposing a version of the trip that would benefit him. The scene's long pause before this line ([16:08] gap) gives it extra resonance — he's been thinking about San Francisco the whole time. Deep character integration.

jokes.text: Post-reconciliation, while lying in bed, Alex asks: 'So do you think we're going to do that mermaid sketch again?' Long pause. Larry: 'I don't—I don't know.'
jokes.setup: They've just had a romantic reconciliation. Alex immediately pivots to her career prospects on the show.
jokes.punchline: The question — in bed, post-intimacy — is 'are we doing the mermaid sketch again?' The question reveals that for Alex, the relationship and the career opportunity are not separable. Larry's long pause is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The episode's comedic and dramatic apex in a single exchange. The mermaid sketch question in bed crystallizes everything the episode is about: Alex's ambition, Larry's paranoia, and the impossibility of separating personal and professional in Hollywood. The long transcript gaps ([16:30], [16:36], [16:41], [16:46], [16:50]) suggest a painfully extended beat before and after Larry's non-answer. Rewatch bonus for how precisely it resolves all the episode's threads in one devastating question.

jokes.text: Alex's follow-up: 'How long is that, a while?' Larry: 'I don't know. A couple months maybe.' Alex: 'You don't care about my career at all, do you?'
jokes.setup: Larry has stalled on the mermaid sketch question; Alex persists with 'how long is a while?'
jokes.punchline: The pivot from romantic aftermath to 'you don't care about my career at all, do you?' — the bedroom negotiation fully unmasked
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'a couple months' to 'you don't care about my career at all' is both dramatically sharp and darkly funny — Larry's commitment to non-commitment finally becomes legally binding evidence against him. The comedy is in the speed of the escalation and the specificity of what she's actually angry about.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I happen to be in love with you.' Pause. 'And, uh... I'm confused.' Longer pause. 'Shit.'
jokes.setup: Alex has accused him of not caring about her career; Larry tries to respond
jokes.punchline: Larry's most romantic declaration — 'I happen to be in love with you' — is immediately undermined by 'And, uh... I'm confused' and ultimately resolved with 'Shit.' as his emotional conclusion
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best comedy-drama moments. 'I happen to be in love with you' is a declaration with 'happen to be' doing enormous emotional distancing — love as something that occurred to him accidentally. 'And I'm confused' contradicts the romance immediately. 'Shit.' as the final word on his emotional state is perfectly calibrated. The pauses are essential — this is Shandling's comedy at its most precise. Deep character integration: only Larry expresses love this way.

jokes.text: Alex says 'I think I've been really there for you.' Larry's response: 'Huh! Right.' (a bitter, dry snort)
jokes.setup: Alex is arguing she's been supportive of Larry
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'Huh! Right.' is a single-breath verdict — dismissive, deeply sarcastic, and entirely unjustified given his behavior all episode
jokes.explanation: A small but very Larry moment — his inability to accept any narrative in which he's not the victim. The irony is rich: he's the one who sabotaged her sketch appearance and can't recognize it. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: The network-planted 'rumor': 'Network rums: Jon Stewart to replace Sanders.' Artie shows it to Larry as a newspaper or trade item.
jokes.setup: Artie uses the rumor as evidence that Roger is actively working against Larry
jokes.punchline: The headline 'Network rums' (likely 'rumbles' truncated) alongside the specific threat of Jon Stewart replacement reads as the show's darkly comedic engagement with its own precarity
jokes.explanation: The show plays its own industry anxieties for dark comedy — using a real name (Jon Stewart) as the replacement threat is meta and specific. Gains rewatch value for anyone who knows the show ends with Larry's replacement.

jokes.text: Artie confronts Roger at a party or event. Roger: 'Don't speak or your fish will get very cold.' Then leaves. Artie: 'Bye-bye.'
jokes.setup: Artie has confronted Roger about working against Larry; Roger responds with a non-sequitur threat about cold fish
jokes.punchline: Roger dismisses Artie's confrontation with the absurd 'your fish will get very cold' — implying they're at a dinner, the fish will go cold, and Artie should prioritize his meal over his boss. Artie's 'Bye-bye' completes the absurdist exchange.
jokes.explanation: Roger's 'your fish will get very cold' is genuinely original — a power-move dismissal that uses cold dinner as a metaphor for irrelevance. The absurdity is that it's both a real concern and a complete deflection. Artie's calm 'Bye-bye' adds to the surreal quality. The bystander's 'That was dramatic. Weird.' validates the audience's reaction within the scene.

jokes.text: After Artie's confrontation with Roger ends bizarrely, a bystander says 'That was dramatic. [nervous chuckle] Weird.'
jokes.setup: Artie has just had a tense, strange confrontation with Roger that ended with fish temperature and 'Bye-bye'
jokes.punchline: The bystander's 'That was dramatic... Weird.' perfectly mirrors the audience's reaction — validating the absurdity
jokes.explanation: A functional audience-surrogate joke — the nervous chuckle followed by 'Weird' is an honest reaction that works as punctuation for the scene. Not exceptional on its own but serves the moment well.

jokes.text: Larry watches himself on TV doing stand-up about his family going to Hawaii. The bit: 'It ended up being The Clampetts go to Maui. 'Cause you get my family together, there is an empty K-Mart somewhere.'
jokes.setup: Larry describes taking his family to Hawaii with 3 million frequent-flyer miles
jokes.punchline: 'The Clampetts go to Maui' as the vacation summary, followed by 'there is an empty K-Mart somewhere' — suggesting the family drains a discount store before any trip
jokes.explanation: Solid stand-up construction. The Beverly Hillbillies reference ('Clampetts go to Maui') is an efficient class-indicator shorthand, and the K-Mart detail is specific enough to land. Good economy, clearly polished material, but not exceptional stand-up.

jokes.text: Stand-up: 'They show up at the airport, they're using coolers and grocery bags for luggage... The skycap was like, "Which one's yours, the Samsonite?" And they were like, "No, we got the igloo with the duct tape on it and the 5 Piggly-Wiggly bags right there."'
jokes.setup: The family is described as using makeshift luggage for a first-class vacation
jokes.punchline: The Igloo cooler with duct tape and Piggly-Wiggly grocery bags as luggage — the specificity of the brands makes the class comedy land
jokes.explanation: The Piggly-Wiggly/Igloo combination is excellent specificity — both regionally coded brands that signal class and geography immediately. The skycap's 'Samsonite?' is a good setup line. Competent professional stand-up with strong detail work.

jokes.text: Stand-up: 'My brother leans over and goes, "You know that ain't them dogs' real voice."' — about Homeward Bound playing on the airplane.
jokes.setup: The movie Homeward Bound is playing on the plane; brother has revelation to share
jokes.punchline: The brother's solemn disclosure that the dogs' voices in Homeward Bound are not the dogs' actual voices — delivered as fresh insight on a film where this is obviously true
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the stand-up section. The comedy is in the total obviousness of what the brother is revealing — Homeward Bound's dogs don't actually talk, this is not a secret — delivered with the earnestness of genuine discovery. The sister's follow-up ('Thanks for spoiling it for everybody else') is the perfect button, treating the revelation as a spoiler. Well-structured, high economy, quotable.

jokes.text: Stand-up button: 'My sister got mad, you know. "Thanks for spoiling it for everybody else."'
jokes.setup: The brother has just revealed that the dogs in Homeward Bound don't really talk
jokes.punchline: The sister treating this as a genuine movie spoiler — getting angry on behalf of the other passengers for having the 'surprise' of non-talking dogs ruined
jokes.explanation: The escalation here is the sister's anger making the joke land twice — first the brother's obliviousness, then the sister's misplaced outrage treating a non-spoiler as a spoiler. The economy is excellent — one line does all the work. Together with Joke 57, this forms the best two-beat sequence in the stand-up section.

tmdb_overview: Larry's relationship with his new girlfriend is threatened when she takes on the ""mermaid"" role in a show skit, and wants to use it as a springboard for her career.
